en: Regarding the *Huayan Tongjiao Wenda* (Explanatory Questions and Answers on the Common Teachings of the Avatamsaka) composed by Master Ketang: its meaning is profound and mysterious, and its phrasing is elegant and abundant;
it truly accords with the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and may be called a work of excellent exposition.
Master Xia'an subsequently compiled what he had heard to distinguish between the erroneous and the correct; yet, failing to grasp the fundamental essence, he could not entirely avoid error.

(Sanghye) Although my learning is meager and limited, I have ventured to provide this clarification not out of a desire to inscribe my name among the great pillars and beams [of the tradition], but rather in the hope that it may help realize the Way of the Xinketang and resolve the doubts of those who study Buddhism. May those who read this take note.
May you be fortunate enough to avoid reproach for this.
Written on the day after the winter solstice in the fourth year of the Qiandao era (the Wuzi year),
by the monk Shihui of Yufeng, who records [this] with joyful faith.
The disciple of Lyi Ze (Sanghye) provides a commentary and asks:

"In the Great Vehicle of the *Avataṃsaka*, there are only the two teachings of 'Identity' and 'Distinction. While the meaning of 'Distinction' is largely consistent with other explanations, the doctrine of 'Ease and Simplicity' (*Iksam*) is particularly unique and is for the most part not followed [by others].

(Iksam says: 'In the initial gate of the Distinct Teaching, scriptural proofs are extensively cited to show that the three and the one are not identical. If one were to provide an explanation in this manner, there might be lands where only the One Vehicle is taught.'"* )"

There may be lands where only the Three Vehicles are taught; in such cases, it would not be called either the "Distinct Teaching" (*biejiao*) or the "Common Teaching" (*tongjiao*). Only when the Three and One are taught together does it receive this latter name. While one might say as much when explaining the *Lotus Sūtra* as a Common Teaching, this is not what is meant here by the "Distinct Teaching of the One Vehicle," which is entirely different from other schools.
Thus it is said: "The majority do not follow [this]. Yangzi stated: "That which does not accord with the laws of the former kings, the gentleman does not take as a model.

If we speak of the One Vehicle as a Common Teaching, some say there are three types: (1) the fusion of the beginning and end within the single Dharma-realm; (2) the harmony of the two, the three, and the one; and (3) the commonality of the sudden and the real. Others speak of four gates (the *Huìjiě* states: first...).

1. Identity through the harmonious integration of the three into one; 2. Identity through the sublation of duality; 3. Identity through similarity of meaning and category; 4. Identity through the total inclusion of all teachings. Some say: "The phrasing differs slightly, but the great meaning does not vary. (Yufeng said:

The *Kongmu* states, 'One gathers the three and returns to the one,' thus we know they are identical. As for the various Patriarchs who speak of 'total inclusion' and 'sublation of duality' and so forth, although their phrasing differs, they do not go beyond this;

therefore it is said that the great meaning does not vary. Yet students are divided, not knowing which is correct. I request the young scholars of talent to extensively consult the texts of the Patriarchs and demonstrate what [the truth] is.
Return! One must adjudicate right and wrong through public principle; one must not privately favor one's own faction. My most earnest prayers!

Regarding the first statement, "A single word universally encompasses": this means that from among many distinct meanings, one takes up a single meaning (the *Kongmu* says: "From among numerous distinct meanings, a single word universally encompasses them";

furthermore, since the meanings encountered differ, from among various dharma-gates, one takes up a single meaning; the others have no separate characteristics). Thus, within the *Avataṃsaka*, the various stages such as faith, understanding, and practice—by means of the single word "faith"—establish the stage of faith. That which is contained within this stage universally establishes understanding, practice, principle, and phenomena.

All such dharma-gates likewise distinguish between the various preceding and succeeding stages, as their dharmic characteristics differ; they also synthesize the realm of the Universal Eye (*puyan*) with the unimpeded *dhāraṇī*-gate of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Based on this sagely artistry within a single word, it is profound upon the profound.

Furthermore, within the categories of "identical" and "distinct," each explains the meanings of identity and distinction (Zhixiang says: Within the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), there is also identity and distinction. Because the many are identical with the one, this is identity. Because the one manifests as the many, this is distinction.

Within the Identical Teaching (*tongjiao*), there is also identity and distinction. That the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles share the same skillful means is identity. That they are distinct according to the specific capacities of sentient beings is distinction).
It is not that the various positions in dispute need not be distinguished.

At the beginning of the chapter: first, the Separate Teaching; second, the Common Teaching. *Yijian* explains: "The subsequent section on the Common Teaching directly addresses the fundamental and derivative aspects of the Dharma-realm as being harmoniously integrated.
Therefore, the following chapter states: 'This Common Teaching explains that all vehicles and so forth are merged and fused into non-duality.'"

"One Dharma-realm. The critique states: "The citations presented here are incomplete" (the Chapter states: "This is the teaching of the Common Vehicle, which harmonizes and integrates all vehicles so that they are non-dual and identical to the single Dharma-realm;

it has two gates: first, the gate of dissolving the provisional to return to the real, which is the One Vehicle teaching; second, the gate of gathering the real to form the provisional, which refers to the teachings of the Three Vehicles and so forth"). Furthermore, this confuses the thesis and the reason. (In the Western Regions, whenever a single principle is explained...)

All [of these] possess the three members of a syllogism (*trirūpa-anumāna*) and are free from the thirty-three fallacies. Now, however, only the *pakṣadharma* (the property of the subject) is cited, while the *hetu* (the reason) is not set forth. This is because [the text] takes the merging of the provisional into the real and the gathering of the real to form the provisional as its reason;

thus it establishes the doctrine of the non-duality of the "Common Teaching" (*sāmānya-naya*). If the reason were submerged [and left unstated], how could one possibly synthesize and harmonize this non-duality? Furthermore, using this very doctrine as the basis for the name of the "Common Teaching"—is this not a confusion of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*)?

[The author] himself says: "This is the gate for those who propagate [the teaching], not the teaching intended for those to be converted. Yi Jian comments: "The establishment of these two gates at the beginning of the chapter constitutes the gate for those who propagate, not the teaching for those to be converted."

Regarding this teaching: if one wishes to apply it to specific capacities, one should follow the "common and distinct" (tongbie) analysis found in the *Great Commentary* (*Dashu*). Furthermore, when our Patriarch established his words to judge the teachings, he did not do so for the sake of specific capacities; moreover, in the subsequent text concerning the common and distinct, there are naturally statements regarding the inclusion of capacities and the accomplishment of benefit.
Welcoming Blessings (Yingfu) comments: "This is an integrated exposition of the three and the one. Thus, the three vehicles and the one vehicle are harmonized and not distinct. [Question:

Regarding this so-called "non-distinction," does it mean that the three vehicles are not distinct from the one vehicle, or that the one vehicle is not distinct from the three vehicles? Furthermore, the Patriarch himself stated: "First, because the three are identical to the one, they are not distinct; second, because the one is identical to the three, they are not distinct. The former belongs to the Separate Teaching and is not the Same Teaching.

Now, when you say the three and the one are not distinct, on what sutra or treatise is this based? Even the *Lotus Sūtra* refutes the three to reveal the one; it is not a case of the three and the one being non-distinct. He further annotates: "This..."

It is called "identical" (*tong*) because the three and the one are present together. (The *Huìjiě* states: "The One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles are harmonized and not different. It also says: "Because the three and the one are present together. Furthermore:

"This is based on the presence of the three and the one. *Xīsīn* says: "The three and the one are explained in conjunction; it is unclear whether these various phrases are identical or different. If they are identical, why are they presented alternately? If they are different, what meaning would be appropriate?

Furthermore, it distinguishes this from the sense of the ocean containing the hundred rivers, and so forth (the distinction from the meaning of the ocean containing the hundred rivers shall be clarified below).

Zhixiang’s commentary states: The Sūtra says, "The three are brought together and returned to the one"; therefore, we know they are identical. The many meanings are as explained there. (Zhixiang says: That which is called "identical" means that the three vehicles are identical with the One Vehicle.

Furthermore, that which is called "identical" means that the Lesser Vehicle is identical with the One Vehicle. Again, that which is called "identical" means that the Lesser Vehicle is identical with the three vehicles, and so forth. If one says the three vehicles are identical with the One Vehicle, then this comprehensively includes both the provisional and the Lesser Vehicles.)

If one says that the Hīnayāna is identical to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), then it would merely include those of the ditches and canals [the lower classes]. Previously it was said that the meaning of "Great" is not in error; now it is said that many meanings are like that. Thus, the preceding and succeeding parts follow one another. It is further stated: "Now, seeking a comprehensive understanding through principle, there is no difference in its趣 (qù—tendency/purpose) from the meaning of 'identical'. "The son is correct and not otherwise. The critique says:
"The 'Easy and Simple' (Yìjiǎn) refers to that distinct teaching (*biéjiào*) to explain this distinction within the correspondence (*duìtóng*).

Now, by taking up that correspondence, it demonstrates that the meaning of this correspondence within the distinction is without error. (That [text] is the *Kǒngmù*; this is the *Jiàozhāng*. Yìjiǎn says: The *Kǒngmù* states that the distinct teaching is distinct from the three...")"

"Riding upon" (the *sheng*) refers to taking the "Distinct Teaching" (*biejiao*) from the "Categorical Categories" (*kongmu*) to explain the "distinctness within the same" (*dui tong zhi bie*) in this current chapter. Yufeng said: "Zhizang’s commentary states: 'The Sūtra says that the three are merged and returned to one; thus we know they are the same.

This takes the 'Same Teaching' (*tongjiao*) from the Categorical Categories to demonstrate the 'sameness within the distinct' (*dui bie zhi tong*) in this current chapter. Question: Previously it was said that the Distinct Teaching is merely "easy, simple, and uniquely different," yet now it is said that its meaning of being "distinct in relation to the same" is not contradictory. Why is there this internal contradiction? Answer: When there was a fault previously, it was rejected; when this can be used here, it is adopted.
What cause for confusion is there? Yingfu also said: "If the meanings of the Distinct are all the same, then they are also identical. (*Huie* [Comprehensive Explanation])

[The Master] said: "Regarding the names and meanings of the Separate Teaching (biejiao), all the Patriarchs are in agreement; thus, this [position] is also accepted. The above concludes the first meaning).
Within the *Qingliang zongxiang hui tong* (The Comprehensive Synthesis of the General Characteristics by Qingliang), it is sometimes divided into four [teachings].

It states therein: 'The third is the Common Teaching of the One Vehicle (tongjiao yicheng), such as the *Lotus Sūtra* and others'. (In the *Qingliang zongxiang hui tong*, it says: "It is sometimes divided into four. This also consists of two gates. First, the three intermediate teachings, which preserve the three and dissolve the two because they are distinct. When expanded, they become four: first, the Separate Teaching of the Hīnayāna, such as the [four... )

1. The *Āgamas* and so forth; 2. The Triyāna of the Shared Teaching, such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and others; 3. The Ekayāna of the Shared Teaching, such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and others; 4. The Ekayāna of the Distinct Teaching, such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. The *Yanyi* commentary explains:

"Regarding 'the three intermediate teachings that preserve the three and merge the two': the Initial, Final, and Sudden teachings are called 'intermediate' because the former has the Hīnayāna and the latter has the Perfect Teaching (Rundiao). Thus they are termed 'intermediate. Among these, the Initial Teaching preserves the three [vehicles], and thus it is established as a distinct teaching.

The Final and Sudden teachings both merge the two [vehicles], and thus they are combined into one teaching. (As listed below among the four, the "Ekayāna of the Shared Teaching" refers precisely to the combination of the Final and Sudden teachings.)

Regarding "Ease and Simplicity" (*yìjiǎn*), in the *Shìjiào zhāngshè yì* (Exegesis on the Compendium of Benefits for the Teachings), under the section on the "Common Vehicle of the One Vehicle" (*tóngjiào yīshèng*), it states:

"This [One Vehicle] is the synthesis of the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle, and thus belongs to the category of the Common Teaching. The aforementioned Separate Teaching of the One Vehicle is the Perfect Teaching (*yuánjiào*);

the provisional teaching of the Three Vehicles is the Initial Teaching (*shǐjiào*); and the Common Teaching of the One Vehicle corresponds to the Final and Sudden Teachings (*zhōngdùn*). Therefore, the *Qīngliáng xuánwén* says: 'Three...'"

The "One Vehicle of Identical Teaching" (tóngjiào yīshéng), such as that found in the *Lotus Sūtra* and others, is explained in the *Yanyi* (*Yanyi shi*) as being the synthesis of the Final and Sudden Teachings.

(Regarding the discrepancy, it should be said: Shanzhu cites this without distinguishing between right and wrong because his intent lies in directly refuting the *Huìjiě*. However, Yìjiǎn cites the *Xuánwén* to prove that the "One Vehicle of Identical Teaching" is included within the "Benefits. Furthermore, while the *Jiàozhāng* assigns the Final and Sudden to the Three Vehicles, the *Xuánwén* assigns the Final and Sudden to the One Vehicle;
thus, citing the One to prove the Three is insufficient for a definitive distinction).
The critique states: This master further points out that this is precisely what the Separate Teaching (biejiao) does not exclude. [Yìjiǎn] says:

"Although the three intermediate teachings are all attained by the three types of persons, the Final and Sudden Teachings ultimately merge and return to a single unity, attaining the fruit of Buddhahood; this is the One Vehicle (ekayāna). The Initial Teaching’s three vehicles have distinct causes for cultivation and thus distinct fruits obtained;

these are strictly limited to the provisional teaching of the three vehicles. Now, this comparative analysis of the three vehicles refers specifically to the provisional gate of the Initial Teaching. [The opponent] raises an objection: "The Huayan One Vehicle is utterly distinct from all other teachings; why then do you specifically exclude the provisional teaching of the three vehicles? [The author] replies: "The meaning of the present text is as follows..."

This is because those who study the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (characteristics of phenomena) do not believe that outside of the Mahāyāna there is a separate One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), and thus they confuse the provisional and the real; therefore, [the text] distinguishes between them. The teachings of the Final and Sudden [Vehicles] are also the One Vehicle, and are not what is being excluded here. Furthermore, it says:

"Although the texts of the Final and Sudden teachings do not explicitly exclude [other vehicles], they are always inherently distinct. [Zhi]yi says: "The Final and Sudden teachings both attain the fruit of Buddhahood, and are thus the One Vehicle.

Since they are called the 'One Vehicle,' yet you say they are 'always inherently distinct'—how can this be? Moreover, the ox-cart on the open plain is one of the four vehicles; how could there be any distinction [between them]? There is no Buddha of the three periods who does not preach these four vehicles. First...

The Śrāvaka-yāna; second, the Pratyekabuddha-yāna; third, the Bodhisattva-yāna; and fourth, the Buddha-yāna. These are called the four vehicles (*catur-yāna*). Furthermore, regarding all the commentaries and treatises by the sages and worthies of the Western Regions and the Eastern Land (China), with the exception of those that open the way for humans and devas, they likewise speak only of these four vehicles.

Moreover, in our own school’s five teachings (*pañca-deśanā*), although there are five teachings, the vehicles are only four categories. This is explained in detail in the section on the opening and closing of the vehicles and teachings.

Furthermore, when Zhizang and Xianshou state that the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is the One Vehicle, it corresponds precisely to that fourth Buddha-vehicle. When Qingliang and Guifeng state that the latter three teachings constitute the One Vehicle, this also corresponds precisely to that fourth Buddha-vehicle. How could there be any difference? Therefore, he points this out, saying:

This refers to the Final and Sudden teachings, not the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). To determine the meaning within this context, it is also said that the Final and Sudden are not the Later Teaching.
Other meanings are not recorded here. The *Yingfu huijie* states:
"The essential point is that the Final and Sudden two teachings equally eliminate duality; therefore, they are called the 'One Vehicle of the Same Teaching' (*tongjiao yicheng*)."

The commentary states: This refers to the convergence of the Final and Sudden Teachings into a single unity; it does not mean that the Final and Sudden Teachings themselves are combined to form a single entity.

It specifically concerns how the Final and Sudden Teachings are identical in their absence of the Two Vehicles, and is therefore termed the "Identical Teaching of the One Vehicle. Furthermore, this is noted in the commentary on the subsequent section.

If the final and sudden [teachings] were identical in their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), how could there be a distinction between the gradual and the sudden? How then could they be the same? Furthermore, it is said:
"It is not that the final and sudden are combined to make them the same; rather, they are called 'the same' because, in terms of their commonality, both are extinguished. Again, it is said:

"People of recent times all claim that the two teachings of the final and the sudden are combined to form the 'same teaching,' while the gradual and the sudden remain distinct. With what, then, would they be combined?"

The critique states: This is also not the same as [the teaching] within the Perfect (Yuan). (Yingfu says: It branches out from the three vehicles of the Shared Teaching; it is not the same as that which exists within the Perfect.

Furthermore, it is not the case that the final and the sudden are combined, nor is it the existence or cessation of their separation. (Combining them results in four teachings, while separating them results in five teachings.

Since it is said they are "not identical" when combined, this refers to the existence or cessation of their separation. The particle *zhi* is a grammatical auxiliary, similar to the usage in the *Zhuangzi*: "the anger of killing-him" or "the anger of deciding-it. Furthermore, it intends to obliterate these two identities.

This explains why it is designated as a teaching of the same category (*tongjiao*). (Yingfu further adds his own commentary, saying: "If one does not take the merging of the two as the reason for its designation, what else could be used? Furthermore, he cites the harmony between the beginning and the end.")

This serves as the reason for the name [of this teaching] being derived from its gradual instruction. Now, let us pose a counter-question. Qingliang says: "Because the Initial Teaching (shijiao) maintains the three vehicles, it is separately established as one teaching. Furthermore, if the Initial Teaching maintains the three vehicles, by what other teaching is it itself subsumed?
Would it not also be granted a name? Other meanings may be understood as they were analyzed during the lecture.

Master Qingliang’s commentary states: "Because the Initial Teaching maintains the three [vehicles], it is established as a separate teaching; because the Final and Sudden Teachings dissolve the duality of these two, they are combined into a single teaching.

As listed below within the four categories, it says: "The third is the One Vehicle of the Shared Teaching," which refers to the combination of the Final and Sudden Teachings (as previously cited in full from the *Yanyi* [Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra], fascicle 6).
The commentary states: This refers to the merging of the two [teachings] into one, which explains the reason why they emerge as a single teaching;

it is not the cause by which the name "Sameness Teaching" (Tongjiao) is established. Therefore, there are four categories: the three teachings preserved as one, the two teachings merged into one, and the Small and Perfect [Teachings].
It is also clearly stated that the One Vehicle of the Sameness Teaching is identical to the Final and Sudden [Teachings], and it accords with the *Yingfu* [treatise].

[This is] different. (Yingfu said: "Because the two [aspects of] cause and condition are extinguished, it is named 'Same Teaching' (*tongjiao*). Yufeng says this explains the reason why they emerge and merge into a single teaching; it is not the reason for the name 'Same Teaching' itself.
Nevertheless, each establishes its own position, so there is no need to harbor doubts.

It is further stated: "Based on whether they are harmoniously integrated (*yuanrong*) or not, two types are distinguished. That is, both the True Teaching (*shijiao*) and the Sudden Teaching (*dunjiao*) are non-integrated, as they constitute the One Vehicle of the Common Teaching (*tongjiao yisheng*).

(This is a selection based on the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena, as cited in full from the *Zhenyuan lu*, Vol. 1, Part 1 and below). Question: If they are entirely non-integrated, how do they differ from the Sudden and True Teachings? Answer:

If one enters the perfect inclusion (*yuan shou*), where principle and phenomena are non-obstructive, there must necessarily be the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena (*shi-shi wuai*). Why is this? Because the four gates, such as non-obstruction and so forth, are all distinct teachings (*biejiao*).
The commentary states: Since it is said that they are not fused to become identical, yet their two names are not extinguished to become identical, is this not manifestly clear?
Furthermore, it is also evident that this One Vehicle of the Identical Teaching (tongjiao yicheng) is a synthesis of the Final and Sudden [teachings].
It is further said: "If self and other are mutually transcended, then one’s mind is of the same substance as the minds of all sentient beings;

"This meaning applies to the Three Vehicles and also extends to the teaching of the One Vehicle" (*Kongmu yuanqi zhang*). It is further stated:

"This passage applies to the Three Vehicles and also extends to the function of the One Vehicle" (*Yao wen sanxing sanwuxing yi*). Again it is said: "This passage pertains to the One Vehicle and extends to the function of those Three Vehicles" (*Yao wen huiguofa yi*).
These are identical in their general interpretation. However, the source of this confusion lies entirely in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Zhilun).

This is the teaching of the shared [vehicle]. Because "shared" (gòng) implies "identical" (tóng), the Grand One employs it and all the patriarchs follow it in common; how could there be any divergent purpose?
Thus we know that the name "shared teaching" (tóngjiào) found in various texts—its interpretation does not go beyond the three meanings of being identical, universal, harmonious, and conjoined.

Because those of the same class are equal to one another, it is called "shared. Since the interpretation is thus established, the various texts mutually complement one another. Now, I wish to demonstrate their meaning.
Let us simply consider this: that the convergence of the three [vehicles] into one is a characteristic of the teaching (*jiao-xiang*).
Since this principle is elucidated within that teaching, we know they are identical; thus, the name and meaning of the "teaching of returning the three and entering the one" can be explained.

How could it be that the convergence of the three into one is itself the definition of the character "identical" (*tong*)? (The *Huijie* explains the four meanings of the "identical teaching," all of which function as definitions for how the name is derived.)
The reason for this is that the meaning of emptiness and non-emptiness is what is elucidated by the two vehicles; it is not the definitive teaching of the beginning and the end.

(However, while the two meanings of emptiness and non-emptiness are clarified by the two vehicles, these are not the grounds upon which the two vehicles derive their names. Therefore, in the present One Vehicle, there are both the shared and the unshared.
The Patriarch said: "Furthermore, regarding the mutual inclusion and harmonious integration of these five teachings, there are five levels.

First, they may be taken as a single whole; that is, the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) subsumes the preceding four, such that each and every one is identical to the Perfect. There is thus only the One Great Skillful Dharma. (The *Jiaozhang* states:

'Or they are taken as a single whole, meaning that the fundamental and the derivative are fused and melted into one, which is the One Great Skillful Dharma. The *Tanyuan*, the *Dashu*, and the *Zhenyuan* all state: 'It is solely the Tathāgata’s one great skillful means for gathering in and transforming sentient beings. The fifth fascicle of the *Cunjiao Yuanjue Daocao* states: 'The Perfect Teaching subsumes the four'...")"

At this time, [each and every thing] is identical to the Perfect (Ichi-ichi-dō-en). It is sometimes called the Perfect Teaching (Enkyō); sometimes called the One Vehicle (Ichijō); sometimes called the Mainstay of the Teachings (Kyōkō); sometimes called the Ocean of Teachings (Kyōkai);

sometimes called the Teaching of the Single Perfect Sound (Icchionkyō); sometimes called the Universal Dharma (Fuhō); and sometimes called the Common Source (Tsūshū) [as stated in the *Kongoku Jigen-shō*]. It is also called the Tree-Treasury of Nature-Arising (*Shōki-jūzō*) [as stated in the *Yōmon Kyōsōgi*:

"The Tree-Treasury of Nature-Arising internally adorns the One Vehicle and externally embellishes the Three Vehicles as well as the Lesser Vehicle"]. It is further called the Great Tree of Dependent Origination (*Engi-daishu*) [as stated in the *Yōmon*].

Regarding the meaning of "before and after attaining Buddhahood," it is said: *If one relies on the teaching of the One Vehicle, one attains Buddhahood in every thought-moment. Throughout all stages—from the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) up to Bodhi—one exhaustively reaches all sentient beings to be transformed.

These attained positions are universally pervasive throughout the realm of sentient beings, without any sequence of before or after, because they constitute a single tree of dependent origination.* It is also called the "School of Infinite Perfect Interpenetration and Sovereignty" (*Kongmu fashu zhang*);
or the "Dharma of Perfect Interpenetration and Sovereignty" (*Kongmu liaojian zhang*); or the "Inexhaustible Buddha-Dharmas"; or "Samantabhadra."

The inexhaustible Dharma is also called the Great Sovereign of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), or the Perfect Teaching, or the Perfect School, or the Complete Treasury, or the Sea of Perfect Perfection.
(The *Śāstra* on Chapter Ten states: "In the Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra, it is said: 'Because the Sea of Perfect Perfection attains the supremacy of all Buddhas;

because no Buddha can fail to achieve the excellence of the Sea of Perfect Perfection. It is also called the Sea of the Perfection of Innate Virtue. (The *Śāstra* on Chapter One states: "Is the Mahāyāna Dharma that which all Buddhas have attained? It is that which they are able to attain...")

Regarding all Buddhas: because the Buddhas do not [attain it] anew, so it is for Bodhisattvas, followers of the Two Vehicles, and all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). This is the ocean of the perfection of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*). It is also called the "Root of Teaching" or the "Dharma-gate of General Characteristics.

(The *Great Sutra Commentary*, Fascicle 3, Part 1, states: "The first Heavenly King attains the Dharma-gate of General Characteristics. When the Buddhas are about to appear, they are all born in that heaven. At the time of their descent, they universally respond to the entire Dharma-realm.")

He suddenly expounded the *Avataṃsaka* as the Perfect Dharma (or it is called the Wheel of the Perfect Teaching; the second fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, the Heavenly King Contentment attained the liberation door of understanding the wheel of the perfect teaching of all Buddhas appearing in the world").
The critique states: All [these teachings] belong to the One Vehicle of the perfect and distinct *Avataṃsaka*, which constitutes the great system that fully subsumes all other doctrines.

It is all-encompassing, harmoniously integrating, endowed with all virtues, and universally penetrating; one may attain them according to whatever name is invoked. (This passage captures the general intent of the comprehensive synthesis;
therefore, various names have been cited as the basis for the classification of teachings. I hope that future generations will take care to apply their minds to this.)

Alternatively, it is divided into two: first, the "Root" (mūla), and second, the "Branch" (anta). [The *Zhang* states: "First is the Root Teaching, meaning the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), for it is the root of all teachings; second is the Branch Teaching, meaning the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), as they flow forth from that.

Alternatively, it is named "Ultimate and Expedient" (*paryavasāna-upāya*). [The *Zhang* states: "Ultimate and Expedient: because the Three Vehicles and the Small Vehicle, when compared to the One Vehicle, are all considered expedients.

Alternatively, it is called the "Three Vehicles and One Vehicle" (*triyāna-ekayāna*). [From the *Kongmu* chapter on the One and Three Vehicles. Alternatively, it is called the "Shared and Unshared Teachings" (*sādhāraṇa-asādhāraṇa-dharma*). [The *Zhilun* identifies the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as the Unshared Teaching, while other sūtras...]
This is the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-deśanā*). It is sometimes called the "Identical yet Distinct," or the "True Vehicle" (*bhūta-yāna*) and the "Skillful Means Vehicle" (*upāya-yāna*).

Alternatively, it is categorized according to the Great and Small Vehicles (as the *Yao-wen* states: "The two vehicles, Great and Small, are divided into two based on their progression from the teaching toward the fruit within the context of skillful means"). Or it is categorized according to the Provisional and the Real. (Regarding the provisional and the real, there are two explanations. First, explaining the provisional and the real in terms of the ultimate skillful means:

among the five teachings, the last one is the ultimate vehicle, while the preceding four teachings constitute the skillful means vehicle. If one asks, 'Since the preceding four teachings themselves possess both the provisional and the real, why are they all considered provisional? The answer is: because their substantial reality was insufficient, they were not so described; yet in all of them, the Buddha-nature exists)."

Because they involve knowledge and vision, they belong to the Three Vehicles and serve as expedient means (*upāya*). From the Zhenguan era onward, the characteristics of the Dharma became increasingly diverse; some took the five natures and three vehicles as real and the one vehicle and one nature as provisional. Their teachings obscured the One Vehicle, yet their doctrines flourished in China.

Consequently, in commentaries such as those on the *Awakening of Faith*, where both words and principles were partially deficient, this meaning was extensively expounded. It was thereby clarified that the One Vehicle and one nature are real, while the Three Vehicles and five natures are provisional.

Within the Five Teachings, the first two are categorized as the Three Vehicles and the latter three as the One Vehicle; both the Final and Sudden teachings clarify the one nature, and for this reason they are judged to enter the One Vehicle. Both Qingliang and Guifeng inherited this tradition, resulting in two distinct theories. Alternatively, it may be distinguished by the "crooked" and the "straight" (referring to Śākyamuni...).

"Sūtra" (jing) refers to teachings that are winding or crooked; "Śamatha-sūtra" (she-na-jing) refers to teachings that are level and straight. Alternatively, it may be categorized according to the gradual and sudden approaches. As the [relevant] chapter states: "This means that one first practices the Hīnayāna and subsequently proceeds toward the Mahāyāna. Because the Great arises from the Small, it is called 'gradual'."
The direct path for bodhisattvas does not proceed from the small to the great; therefore, it is called "sudden" (*dun*).
The commentary states: All of these are the opening of the preceding One Vehicle Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

However, some first open the unique One Vehicle (*buping yisheng*), and subsequently distinguish between the small and the great, the provisional and the real (first opening the unique [One Vehicle], then, within the common teachings, distinguishing between the small and the great, and further, within the Great Vehicle, distinguishing between the provisional and the real); others first analyze the small.

Regarding the vehicles (*yāna*), there is a subsequent classification of the provisional and the real, and their commonality or distinctness. (First, the non-common [teachings] of the *Hīnayāna* are opened up; next, the provisional and the real are distinguished. The first one is the provisional, and the latter three are the real. Within the single reality, they are further divided into the common and the distinct.

The former two constitute the One Vehicle of Common Teaching (*sāmānya-ekayāna*), and the latter one constitutes the One Vehicle of Distinct Teaching (*viśeṣa-ekayāna*). Alternatively, it is presented as the One Vehicle. (The One Vehicle has two types: first, the One Vehicle of Common Teaching; second, the One Vehicle of Distinct Teaching. Or it is presented as three.
Since the "one" opens up the "two," there are many variations within them. However, various common teachings may also be termed...
Regarding the three vehicles (*triyāna*), they are sometimes called "one" (*ekayāna*). This is because the single vehicle is common to those three vehicles;

even the *hīnayāna* is subsumed within the *ekayāna* solely through the turning of wisdom (*jñānapariṇāmanā*). (From the "Chapter on True Suchness" in the *Kongmu*). This is merely a designation used for convenience. Question:

When various provisional vehicles (*upāyayāna*) are termed the "One Vehicle," is it precisely that [ultimate One Vehicle]? (The word "no" [in the original] is a term of uncertainty. When various provisional vehicles are termed the "One Vehicle," is it the ultimate *ekayāna*, or...)
"Is it not the ultimate One Vehicle (Ekayāna)? Answer: There are two senses. First, it is established by relying on the teaching of the ultimate One Vehicle. Why?
Because it flows from the One Vehicle and is designated by the teaching of the One Vehicle; there is no difference in substance.
Second, it serves as a skillful means (*upāya*) for that ultimate, perfect One Vehicle. Therefore, it is said that the One Vehicle is not itself the perfectly penetrating self-nature.

This is the meaning (Kongmu: Because one proceeds toward the Dharma-gate by relying on expedient means; it is distinguished into two meanings based on the differentiation between identity and non-identity).

Alternatively, it may be divided into three: the Hīnayāna, the Triyāna, and the Ekayāna; or [into categories such as] the gradual and the sudden (Guangtong established "gradual, sudden, and perfect," while Zhizang’s *Souxuan* employs this).

The critique states: Regarding the first meaning, there are two interpretations within the context of the five teachings. If all three [vehicles] are intended for the three types of practitioners, then the middle three constitute the three [vehicles] (as in the *Tanchuan Jiaozhang*, *Kongmu Wen-da*, and other such works).
If, however, the two [lower vehicles] are subsumed into one, then the latter three are all one (as in the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Commentary on the Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*).

Therefore, among the four [types of] One Vehicle of the same teaching (*tongjiao*), it may emerge from the three; that is, within the common teaching (*gongjiao*), it is categorized according to whether the three are preserved or the two are subsumed.

[The same. Dividing it into two, or taking one as the source—(combining the latter three as the Real [shí] and dividing them into two, there are thus the identical and distinct One Vehicles)—therefore, in the *Zhenyuan* [Catalogue], the provisional and real were extensively opened while still maintaining the Small Vehicle, resulting in thirty articles that distinguish the provisional;
subsequently, within the single Real, the identical and distinct [Vehicles] were opened. (*Zhenyuan*, Vol. 1, Part A).
Alternatively, they may be divided into four: namely, the distinct teaching of the Hīnayāna, up to the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle, or the small gradual [teaching], and so forth.

(*Tanxuan ji* states: "Alternatively, they are divided into four, which has two meanings. First, within the aforementioned common teaching, by distinguishing between the preservation of three and the merging of two, two teachings are opened up, thus making four: first, the distinct teaching of the Hīnayāna; second, the common teaching of the Three Vehicles, such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*;

third, the common teaching of the One Vehicle, such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; and fourth, the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle, such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. Second, by distinguishing between the gradual and sudden teachings through the progression of stages and the absence of stages, four are made: first, the Hīnayāna teaching; second, the gradual teaching; third, the sudden teaching; and fourth, the perfect teaching.)

The commentary states: To examine the original meaning and discuss the general principles, there are only three schools. The distinct teaching of the Hīnayāna, which does not extend to Bodhisattvas, is called the Hīnayāna school.
The common teaching of the Three Vehicles, wherein the three types of practitioners alike receive the instruction, is called the Triyāna school.
Directly revealing the fundamental Dharma and synthesizing the three vehicles into one is called the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) school.

However, among the five teachings, the second patriarchs—Qingliang and Guishan—mostly adopt the approach of "submerging the two" to belong to the one, thereby distinguishing it from the provisional; they hold that the latter three [teachings] are all real, naming them the One Vehicle school.

They do not treat "integration" as the same, but rather take integration as the distinction [between schools]. (The first volume of the *Zhenyuan lu* has already been cited previously. [The fourth and fifth... (Yunhua...)

The Second Patriarch, Xianshou, consistently categorized the middle [teachings] as belonging to the Three Vehicles (Triyāna) school, while the final, ultimate [teaching] constituted the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) school.
The Fifth Patriarch, in turn, distinguished between the sudden and the real by positing the "preservation of three" and the "extinction of two," thereby assigning them to the One Vehicle school.

(Investigating the Profundities, Part 1) Therefore, after the fifth and sixth patriarchs divided [the teachings] into three, they all proceeded from those three schools, distinguishing between their similarities and differences to establish the four teachings.

(In the *Tanyuan* and the *Dashi*, both within the context of the "Shared Teachings," they distinguish two teachings based on the preservation of three, the merging of two, and the opening of two; thus they are divided into four.

This is because within the One Vehicle school itself there are two [aspects]. For this reason, some take the fifth as distinct, while the preceding four are collectively designated as the Shared Teaching.

Regarding the vehicles (*yāna*): therein are found the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), and the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Alternatively, one may further distinguish between the non-common Small Vehicle and the common teaching of the Three Vehicles.
As for the remaining teachings on the *tathāgatagarbha* and Buddha-nature that sublate duality, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* treats them as the common teaching of the One Vehicle;

this accords perfectly in both name and substance with the present "perfect opening" of the four teachings. This is because, among the various common teachings, the upper and lower [levels] correspond to one another.

Regarding "mutuality" (*wang*): there is naturally both the common and the uncommon. (To explain the meaning of the boundaries of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*): among the various common teachings, when viewed from higher to lower, there are both common and uncommon aspects.

For example, the teaching of the *Hīnayāna* asserts that the three time periods exist, whereas this is not the case for the *Triyāna*. Conversely, what exists in the *Triyāna* teaching may not exist in the *Hīnayāna*. Or, there are things common to both [the *Dviyāna* and *Triyāna*], such as the shared names and categories of the *bodhipākṣika-dharmas*. Or, there are things absent in both [the *Dviyāna* and *Triyāna*], which refers precisely to the *Ekayāna* teaching.

If one were to analyze the sudden and real [teachings] as that which is excluded, they would all belong to the provisional (*upāya*), falling within the scope of the *Triyāna*, and would consequently be dispersed.
There are five [categories]. The last one possesses both common and distinct aspects within itself, constituting the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) school.

Thus, the One Vehicle itself still has common and distinct aspects; it also accords with the three schools. Therefore, within the One Vehicle, there is no duality of "common" (sāmānya) as opposed to "distinct" (viśeṣa).

Consequently, that which is sudden and real belongs to the Three Vehicles as provisional, while it belongs to the One Vehicle as real—thus departing from the partial and merging with the perfect. This is because of the teaching...
Within the ocean, there are many skillful means for guiding sentient beings according to their capacities; these vary in their numerical categories.

The various masters of past generations each expounded one particular gate (as analyzed in the section on the Establishment of the Teachings in Ancient and Modern Times). Our Patriarch, however, encompassed them all to form a comprehensive web of the teachings; thus, there are instances of both opening and closing.

Although he established many teachings, they were all developed by first perfecting [the teaching] and then gradually unfolding it from within. If this is so, it is also the beginning of the Perfect Teaching.
"Small indeed," he replied. "It is truly so; it is both general and particular. Furthermore, why would one depart from the partial to unite with the perfect?

Because capacities have both universal and particular aspects, and wisdom possesses both the three and the one; since their attainments and orientations differ, the unfolding and rolling up [of the teachings] cannot be said to have a single aspect.

Unfolding while always rolled up, and rolling up while being immediately unfolded—this mastery over unfolding and rolling up constitutes the great principle of the Flower Garland (Avataṃsaka) teaching-net."
Thus ends the "Notes on Questions and Answers Concerning the Shared Teaching."
